# Book I, Proposition 34

*Opposite sides and angles of a parallelogram*

> In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the diameter bisects the areas.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/34-idea.svg" alt="In a parallelogram the opposite sides are equal (blue, red), the opposite angles are equal (yellow, black), and the diagonal cuts it into two equal halves." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>In a parallelogram the opposite sides are equal (blue, red), the opposite angles are equal (yellow, black), and the diagonal cuts it into two equal halves.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/34.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.34, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ACDB be a parallelogrammic area, and BC its diameter;

I say that the opposite sides and angles of the parallelogram ACDB are equal to one another, and the diameter BC bisects it.

For, since AB is parallel to CD,

and the straight line BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Again, since AC is parallel to BD,

and BC has fallen upon them,

the alternate angles ACB, CBD are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Therefore ABC, DCB are two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two angles DCB, CBD respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely that adjoining the equal angles and common to both of them, BC;

therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides respectively, and the remaining angle to the remaining angle; [I. 26]

therefore the side AB is equal to CD,

and AC to BD,

and further the angle BAC is equal to the angle CDB.

And, since the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD,

and the angle CBD to the angle ACB,

the whole angle ABD is equal to the whole angle ACD. [C.N. 2]

And the angle BAC was also proved equal to the angle CDB.

Therefore in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another.

I say, next, that the diameter also bisects the areas.

For, since AB is equal to CD,

and BC is common,

the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively;

and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;

therefore the base AC is also equal to DB,

and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB. [I. 4]

Therefore the diameter BC bisects the parallelogram ACDB.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop34.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop34.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the
diameter bisects the areas. -/
theorem Prop34 {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A C D B) :
    ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ ∧ ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B ∧ ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D ∧
      △ A B C = △ D C B := by
  -- Let ACDB be a parallelogrammic area, and BC its diameter;
  have hBC : B ≠ C := h.2.symm.triangle.ne₁₃
  -- I say that the opposite sides and angles of the parallelogram ACDB are equal to one
  -- another, and the diameter BC bisects it.
  -- For, since AB is parallel to CD,
  have hpar₁ : AreParallel A B C D := h.2.symm.swap_left
  -- and the straight line BC has fallen upon them,
  have hAD : OppositeSidesOf A D B C := hpar₁.oppositeSidesOf h.sameSideOf.symm
  -- the alternate angles ABC, BCD are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hABC_BCD : ∠ A B C = ∠ B C D := Prop29.alternate hpar₁ hAD
  -- Again, since AC is parallel to BD,
  have hpar₂ : AreParallel A C B D := h.1.swap_right
  -- and BC has fallen upon them,
  have hAD_CB : OppositeSidesOf A D C B := hAD.swap
  -- the alternate angles ACB, CBD are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hACB_CBD : ∠ A C B = ∠ C B D := Prop29.alternate hpar₂ hAD_CB
  -- Therefore ABC, DCB are two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two
  -- angles DCB, CBD respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely that adjoining the
  -- equal angles and common to both of them, BC;
  have hABC : Triangle A B C := hpar₁.triangle
  have hDCB : Triangle D C B := hpar₁.symm.swap_left.swap_right.triangle
  have hDC : D ≠ C := hpar₁.2.1.symm
  have hAC : A ≠ C := hpar₂.1
  have hB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D C B := hABC_BCD.trans (angle_symm hBC hDC)
  have hC : ∠ B C A = ∠ C B D := (angle_symm hBC hAC).trans hACB_CBD
  -- therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides
  -- respectively, and the remaining angle to the remaining angle; [I. 26]
  obtain ⟨hAB_DC, hAC_DB, -, hBAC_CDB⟩ :=
    Prop26 hABC hDCB hB hC (Or.inl (len_symm B C))
  -- therefore the side AB is equal to CD,
  have hAB_CD : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖ := hAB_DC.trans (len_symm D C)
  -- and AC to BD,
  have hAC_BD : ‖A C‖ = ‖B D‖ := hAC_DB.trans (len_symm D B)
  -- and further the angle BAC is equal to the angle CDB.
  have hBAC : ∠ B A C = ∠ C D B := hBAC_CDB
  -- And, since the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD,
  -- and the angle CBD to the angle ACB,
  -- the whole angle ABD is equal to the whole angle ACD. [C.N. 2]
  /- BC falls within both angles: C within the angle ABD, and B within the
     angle ACD, as `Parallelogram.sameSideOf` says of the parallelogram named
     from each corner. -/
  have hABD : ∠ A B D = ∠ A B C + ∠ C B D :=
    angle_add_of_within h.rotate.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf h.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf.symm.swap
  have hACD : ∠ A C D = ∠ A C B + ∠ B C D :=
    angle_add_of_within h.sameSideOf.symm.swap h.rotate.sameSideOf
  have hABD_ACD : ∠ A B D = ∠ A C D := by
    rw [hABD, hACD, add_comm (∠ A C B)]
    exact CommonNotion2 hABC_BCD hACB_CBD.symm
  -- And the angle BAC was also proved equal to the angle CDB.
  -- Therefore in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one
  -- another.
  refine ⟨hAB_CD, hAC_BD, hBAC, hABD_ACD, ?_⟩
  -- I say, next, that the diameter also bisects the areas.
  -- For, since AB is equal to CD,
  have hBA_CD : ‖B A‖ = ‖C D‖ := (len_symm B A).trans hAB_CD
  -- and BC is common,
  have hBC_CB : ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := len_symm B C
  -- the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively;
  have : ‖A B‖ = ‖D C‖ ∧ ‖B C‖ = ‖C B‖ := ⟨hAB_DC, hBC_CB⟩
  -- and the angle ABC is equal to the angle BCD;
  have : ∠ A B C = ∠ D C B := hB
  -- therefore the base AC is also equal to DB,
  /- I.4 takes the corner of the given angle first: BAC and CDB, as in I.33. -/
  obtain ⟨hAC_DB', hBAC_CDB_area, -, -⟩ := Prop4 hABC.bac hDCB.bac hBA_CD hBC_CB hB
  -- and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB. [I. 4]
  have harea : △ A B C = △ D C B := by
    rw [area_bac A B C, hBAC_CDB_area, area_bac C D B]
  -- Therefore the diameter BC bisects the parallelogram ACDB.
  exact harea
  -- Q. E. D.

/-- The diameter bisects the parallelogram, said of its area: the parallelogram
`ABCD`, measured by its diameter `AC`, is double the triangle `ABC`. I.35–I.47 cite
I.34 for this ("the triangle ABC is half of the parallelogram EBCA; for the diameter
AB bisects it"). To halve by the other diameter, name the parallelogram from the
next corner (`Parallelogram.rotate`) and turn its area round with
`Parallelogram.quadArea_rotate`. [I. 34] -/
theorem Prop34.bisect {A B C D : Point} (h : Parallelogram A B C D) :
    quadArea A B C D = △ A B C + △ A B C := by
  have hhalf : △ B A C = △ D C A :=
    (Prop34 (A := B) (B := A) (C := C) (D := D) h.rotate).2.2.2.2
  unfold quadArea
  rw [area_cba A C D, ← hhalf, ← area_bac A B C]
```

## Mishnah

**Parallelogrammic areas.** Heath observes that "when parallelograms have to be mentioned for the first time, Euclid calls them 'parallelogrammic areas'" (vol. 1, p. 325), and gathers from Proclus that the word was Euclid's own, suggested by I.33. Euclid never defines the figure. Our `Parallelogram` says both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, the corners taken in order round the figure: here A, C, D, B.

**Two triangles, then their areas.** The diameter BC falls on each pair of parallel sides, and I.29 makes two pairs of alternate angles equal. With BC common, I.26 gives the remaining sides and the remaining angle, and Common Notion 2 adds the angles at B and at C into the other pair of opposite angles. For the areas Euclid goes back to I.4, since I.26 says nothing of them. Heath's DCB, for the Greek's BCD, keeps the corners in order, as he explains under I.33, and our I.26 takes them so.

**What Lean made us say.** `Parallelogram.sameSideOf` puts the far corners on one side of each side, and from that `AreParallel.oppositeSidesOf` puts A and D on opposite sides of BC, so that the angles at B and C are alternate. Named from each corner in turn, the parallelogram also puts BC within the angles ABD and ACD, and `angle_add_of_within` adds the angles there. The conclusion speaks of the triangles ABC and DCB; later proofs cite `Prop34.bisect`, which makes the parallelogram twice either half. The Lean cites just Euclid's three brackets. Postulates 1 and 2 come in where `Prop29.alternate` sets out I.29's figure; I.26 and I.29 bring in both as well, I.4 Postulate 1, and I.29 Postulate 5.

**What a diameter bisects.** Proclus finds the first part of the enunciation general, true of parallelograms alone, and the second not, for a diameter bisects circles and ellipses too: "the ancients, after investigating the fact that the diameter bisects an ellipse, a circle, and a parallelogram respectively, proceeded to investigate what was common to these cases" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 325). Heath doubts it: Proclus must take the figure to be four-sided in the first part, since some regular polygons have their opposite sides and angles equal too, and then he may in the second. Heath places here an-Nairīzī's way of dividing a straight line into equal parts, which uses I.33 and I.34 (vol. 1, p. 326).

**The modern way.** As vectors, D = B + C − A, and the half-turn X ↦ B + C − X about the middle of BC exchanges B and C and takes A to D. It carries the triangle ABC onto DCB and the angle ABD onto DCA, keeping every length, angle and area: the whole of I.34 at once.

## Further reading

- For the half-turn of the modern way, I. M. Yaglom's [*Geometric Transformations I*](https://doi.org/10.5948/UPO9780883859254) (1962), ch. I, §2, "Half Turn and Rotation", in Allen Shields' translation, a slim, playful classic that puts each motion to work on clever constructions.
- For why one motion that keeps every length, angle and area says so much, Felix Klein's ["A comparative review of recent researches in geometry"](https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.3161) (1893, free online), his Erlangen Programme of 1872 in M. W. Haskell's translation, the short manifesto behind the idea that a geometry is defined by the motions it allows.
